content: The antiviral activity of abacavir against HIV-1 was evaluated using various laboratory strains and clinical isolates. Specifically, its efficacy was tested against a T-cell tropic laboratory strain (HIV-1IIIB) in lymphoblastic cell lines, a monocyte/macrophage tropic strain (HIV-1BaL) in primary monocytes/macrophages, and clinical isolates in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. The effective concentration (EC50) of abacavir ranged from 1.8 μM to 4.9 μM against eight clinical isolates. Ribavirin, at a concentration of 50 μM, did not affect the anti-HIV-1 activity of abacavir in cell culture. The antiviral activity of lamivudine against HIV-1 was assessed in various cell lines, including monocytes and fresh human peripheral blood lymphocytes, using standard susceptibility assays. The EC50 of lamivudine ranged from 0.002 to 0.023 μg/mL (0.01 to 0.068 μM) in laboratory studies. In clinical isolates, the EC50 was approximately 0.12 μM in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Lamivudine demonstrated a 5-fold reduction in susceptibility in MT-4 cells when resistance mutations were present. The combination of abacavir and lamivudine exhibited antiviral activity in cell culture against non-subtype B isolates and HIV-2 isolates, with similar efficacy to subtype B isolates. This combination showed additive to synergistic activity when used with other antiretroviral agents, including nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) such as emtricitabine, stavudine, tenofovir, zalcitabine, and zidovudine; non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) such as delavirdine, efavirenz, and nevirapine; protease inhibitors (PIs) such as amprenavir, indinavir, lopinavir, nelfinavir, ritonavir, and saquinavir; and the fusion inhibitor enfuvirtide. However, ribavirin, when used in combination with interferon for hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment, reproducibly reduced the anti-HIV-1 potency of abacavir/lamivudine by 2to 6-fold in cell culture. HIV-1 isolates with reduced susceptibility to the combination of abacavir and lamivudine have been selected in cell culture and obtained from patients failing abacavir/lamivudine-containing regimens. Genotypic analysis of resistant viruses identified amino acid substitutions M184V/I, K65R, L74V, and Y115F in the HIV-1 reverse transcriptase (RT) enzyme. These substitutions were associated with resistance to abacavir and lamivudine. Specifically, the M184V/I substitution, which involves a change from methionine to either isoleucine or valine at codon 184, was the most commonly observed mutation in lamivudine-treated subjects. In a clinical trial involving therapy-naive adults receiving abacavir 600 mg once daily or 300 mg twice daily, both in combination with lamivudine 300 mg and efavirenz 600 mg once daily, the incidence of virologic failure at 48 weeks was similar between the two groups (11% in both arms). Genotypic and phenotypic analyses of virologic failure isolates from this trial revealed the emergence of RT substitutions K65R, L74V, Y115F, and M184V/I during abacavir/lamivudine therapy. The M184V/I substitution was the most frequently observed mutation in virologic failure isolates, occurring in 56% of subjects receiving once-daily therapy and 40% of those receiving twice-daily therapy. Cross-resistance among NRTIs has been observed. Viruses containing resistance-associated substitutions to abacavir and lamivudine, such as K65R, L74V, M184V, and Y115F, exhibit cross-resistance to other NRTIs, including didanosine, emtricitabine, lamivudine, tenofovir, and zalcitabine. The K65R substitution confers resistance to abacavir, didanosine, emtricitabine, lamivudine, stavudine, tenofovir, and zalcitabine. The L74V substitution confers resistance to abacavir, didanosine, and zalcitabine. The M184V substitution confers resistance to abacavir, didanosine, emtricitabine, lamivudine, and zalcitabine. The combination of abacavir/lamivudine has shown reduced susceptibility to viruses with the K65R substitution, with or without the M184V/I substitution, as well as to viruses with the L74V plus M184V/I substitutions. Additionally, viruses with thymidine analog mutations (TAMs) such as M41L, D67N, K70R, L210W, T215Y/F, and K219E/R/H/Q/N, in combination with M184V, also exhibit reduced susceptibility to abacavir. An increasing number of TAMs is associated with a progressive reduction in abacavir susceptibility.
